item.title: NetFlow and SNMP Analytics for Splunk (Preview) - v0.1.4 [Version Update]
item.description:
Platform: Splunk


Release Notes:
## Initial Preview release This is the first public release of the NetFlow and SNMP Analytics for Splunk (Preview) app: a ground-up redesign of NetFlow Logic's Splunk app, rebuilt on Dashboard Studio in dark mode. It is published alongside the current [NetFlow and SNMP Analytics for Splunk](https://splunkbase.splunk.com/app/489) app so teams can evaluate the redesign side by side on the same instance. This Preview will eventually be merged into app 489 as its next major release. ## What's included * **Rebuilt on Dashboard Studio, dark mode.** Every dashboard uses Splunk's modern dashboarding framework. * **19 focused dashboards** replacing roughly 80 fragmented legacy dashboards, organized into a streamlined navigation: a default Overview plus Network Conversations, Infrastructure Health, and Configuration sections. * **Redesigned Network Conversations.** A single consolidated conversation view with a Sankey group-by flow map and a unified detail table, replacing several legacy per-dimension dashboards. * **New interactive Network Topology.** Walk-the-graph exploration built on Splunk 10.4's native `networkgraph` visualization: start from a device and expand its neighbours incrementally. * **Unified Device Health and TCP Health.** SNMP CPU, memory, and interface health consolidated into single dashboards. * **Multi-cloud and flow-format coverage** carried over from the current app: NetFlow v5/v9, sFlow, IPFIX, plus AWS, Azure, GCP, and OCI flow logs, with NFO enrichment (DNS, VM names, GeoIP, IP reputation, application ID, user identity). * **Standardised filters and terminology** across every dashboard. ## Requirements * NetFlow Optimizer (NFO) 2.12.1 or later * Technology Add-on for NetFlow (TA-netflow), installed before this app * Splunk Common Information Model (CIM) 5.x or 6.x * Splunk Enterprise or Splunk Cloud. Splunk 10.4 is required for full functionality; all dashboards except Network Topology also run on Splunk 9.4.1+. ## Known limitations * **Network Topology requires Splunk 10.4.** On Splunk 9.4.1 the topology dashboard is unavailable; every other dashboard functions normally. * **Preview status.** This release is intended for evaluation. Interfaces, dashboard layouts, and the internal app context may change before the redesign is merged into app 489. ## Feedback Please send feedback and issues from the preview period to [team\_splunk@netflowlogic.com](mailto:team_splunk@netflowlogic.com).


Short Description:
Get the network traffic and device health data Splunk can't see on its own. NetFlow Optimizer turns raw NetFlow, IPFIX, sFlow, and SNMP telemetry into enriched, analysis-ready data in Splunk across on-premises and multi-cloud, closing blind spots in network, security, and device-health monitoring.


Description:
NetFlow and SNMP Analytics for Splunk (Preview), built by NetFlow Logic, an official Splunk Partner, is the next-generation redesign of our network and security analytics app, rebuilt on Splunk Dashboard Studio. It gives network and security teams the network traffic and device health data Splunk can't see on its own, with real-time visibility across on-premises and multi-cloud environments. Powered by NetFlow Optimizer (NFO), the app processes all major flow formats (NetFlow v5/v9, sFlow, IPFIX) and cloud flow logs from AWS, Microsoft Azure, Google Cloud Platform, and Oracle Cloud Infrastructure. NFO enriches and filters this telemetry before it reaches Splunk, turning raw flow and SNMP data into analysis-ready intelligence and doing it efficiently, so you close the blind spots in your monitoring without a spike in ingest. What's new in this Preview: - Rebuilt on Dashboard Studio: a modern, faster, dark-mode interface - Streamlined navigation: consolidated from ~80 legacy dashboards into 19 focused, production-quality dashboards - Interactive network topology: walk-the-graph exploration built on Splunk 10.4's native network graph visualization - Unified device health and TCP health views - Same NFO-powered enrichment and multi-cloud coverage you rely on today What you can do with this app: - Monitor your entire network in one place — unified visibility across on-premises infrastructure and all major cloud platforms - Detect threats faster — correlate flow data with IP reputation, GeoIP, user identity, and application context to surface anomalies and suspicious activity - Reduce Splunk ingest costs — filter and aggregate flows upstream in NFO so only enriched, relevant data reaches Splunk - Optimize network performance — identify overloaded interfaces, bandwidth hogs, and congestion before they impact users - Monitor device health with SNMP — poll devices and receive traps (SNMPv2c and v3) for real-time CPU, memory, and interface monitoring - Enrich your data automatically — DNS names, VM names, GeoIP, application identification, and user identity added at ingest Solution areas: Traffic overview and executive dashboards · NetFlow and flow analysis (v5/v9, sFlow, IPFIX) · Cloud flow analytics (AWS, Azure, GCP, OCI) · SNMP device and interface health · Security and threat detection · Administration and configuration Requirements: NetFlow Optimizer (NFO) 2.12.1 or later is required. Compatible with Splunk Enterprise and Splunk Cloud, Splunk ES, and Splunk ITSI (via the Content Pack for SNMP and NetFlow). Start a free 60-day trial at netflowlogic.com/free-trial — or request a demo to see the app running against live network data.

Deslicer AI Insights Add-on is the real-time configuration observation layer for the Deslicer Automation Platform (DAP) — giving Splunk administrators live visibility into the configuration state of every host in their deployment, and unlocking AI-driven automation across the entire Splunk estate. The Insights Add-on runs on all Splunk Enterprise hosts — indexers, search heads, heavy forwarders, and cluster managers — continuously observing and reporting configuration state to the DAP Observer. This real-time stream of configuration intelligence is what enables DAP to detect drift the moment it happens, power AI-driven change recommendations, and safely execute audited deployments with human approval at every step. All events are indexed with CIM-compliant field extractions (sourcetype: deslicer:insights:node), mapped to the Change, Authentication, and Application State data models — ready for Enterprise Security, custom correlation searches, and CIM-based reporting out of the box. On search heads and SHC members, enable the add-on in Splunk Web to access the Insights Node Monitoring dashboard — visibility into the health, activity, and status of every collector node across your fleet. Agents automate daily health checks, GDI onboarding, deployment planning, and more. Every change requires explicit human approval with cryptographic signing and a full audit trail. Deslicer runs fully on-premises (Kubernetes, Docker, air-gapped) or as SaaS — your data stays inside your perimeter when required. Product(s) Enabled: Cisco AI Defense Cisco Duo Cisco Email Threat Defense (ETD) Cisco Endpoint Visibility Module (EVM) CIM Mappings (Beta) Cisco Identity Intelligence (CII) Cisco Multicloud Defense Cisco NVM Cisco Secure Endpoint Cisco Secure Firewall (FTD/eStreamer/ASA) Cisco Secure Workload Cisco Isovalent Cisco Isovalent Edge Processor **Alpha Cisco Secure Malware Analytics (SMA) Cisco Secure Network Analytics (SNA) Cisco Vulnerability Intelligence Cisco XDR (Incident Import & Promote to ES Notable) Here’s the revised version with the sourcetype list and stronger 3.x transition language. **MAJOR VERSION CHANGE: CiscoSecurityCloud 4.0.0 Release Notes** CiscoSecurityCloud 4.0.0 introduces expanded Cisco Secure Firewall / FTD syslog and Advanced Logging support, with improved parsing, event routing, CIM/data model alignment, dashboard visibility, and ingestion reliability. This release adds a new FTD sourcetype routing model that separates FTD events by event family instead of keeping all events under a single generic `cisco:ftd:syslog` sourcetype. This improves field extraction accuracy, dashboard filtering, data model mapping, and long-term supportability for FTD syslog and Advanced Logging data. Because this changes how FTD events are categorized, **4.0.0 may be a breaking change for customers with custom Splunk content**. Content that may require review includes: - Saved searches, alerts, reports, and dashboards that filter only on `sourcetype="cisco:ftd:syslog"` - Custom macros, eventtypes, tags, and CIM/data model constraints - Custom props/transforms or routing assumptions for FTD syslog - Data model acceleration searches scoped to the previous FTD sourcetype - External integrations or correlation searches that expect all FTD events in one sourcetype Customers should update broad FTD searches from "cisco:ftd:syslog" to cisco:ftd:intrusion cisco:ftd:connection cisco:ftd:connection:security cisco:ftd:file cisco:ftd:malware cisco:ftd:discovery cisco:ftd:useractivity cisco:ftd:correlation cisco:ftd:intrusionpacket cisco:ftd:adv:http cisco:ftd:adv:ftp cisco:ftd:adv:conn cisco:ftd:adv:dns cisco:ftd:adv:weird cisco:ftd:adv:notice CiscoSecurityCloud 4.0.0 is intended for customers who want the new FTD Advanced Logging model and are ready to validate custom content against the expanded sourcetypes. To ease the transition, the CiscoSecurityCloud 3.x branch will be actively maintained and should remain the recommended stable branch for customers who require the existing FTD sourcetype behavior. Customers can continue using 3.x while they assess 4.0.0, update custom SPL, and validate dashboards, alerts, and data model acceleration.

item.description:
Platform: Splunk


Release Notes:
## SCIP v1.2.10 — FedRAMP VDR/VER Reporting and PCI DSS 4.0.1 Compliance Accuracy Remediation Cumulative release covering all changes since v1.2.5 (build 247). Adds FedRAMP Vulnerability Detection and Response (VDR) / Vulnerability Evaluation and Reporting (VER) support to the Monthly ConMon Package Builder, and remediates eleven compliance-accuracy defects identified by audits against the published PCI DSS v4.0.1 standard and FedRAMP's current continuous-monitoring rules. **SCIP-141 — FedRAMP VDR/VER reporting:** * New FedRAMP VDR/VER Vulnerability Report section in the Monthly ConMon Package Builder, reframing KEV-matched vulnerabilities from the BOD 26-04 classification engine into FedRAMP's VER language: exploitability (LEV/NLEV), internet reachability (IRV/NIRV), Potential Agency Impact N-rating (PAIN, N1-N5), and the mitigation/remediation timeframe (VDR-TFR-PVR). Implements the eleven required reporting items of VER-RPT-VDT and is exportable for monthly human-readable reporting (VER-TFR-MHR). * New lookups/fedramp\_vdr\_ver\_pain\_matrix.csv (16 rows) with a selectable FedRAMP certification class, open and auditable against FedRAMP's own published timeframe tables. Certification class materially changes remediation windows (for a PAIN-4 internet-reachable finding: 8 days at Class B, 2 days at Class D). * Applications with no public-exposure tag are treated as internet-reachable rather than silently assumed safe — the conservative posture FedRAMP's model requires. Panels include an explicit proxy disclosure stating which values are provisional proxies (IRV from the customer-declared exposure tag, PAIN from BOD 26-04 technical impact) and which require provider attestation, so the report cannot be mistaken for an assessment SCIP is not in a position to make. * Reportable-incident candidates (VER-TFR-IRI) and findings approaching the 192-day accepted-risk threshold (VER-TFR-MAV) are surfaced directly. Mandatory for FedRAMP-certified offerings by December 7, 2026, with the grace period ending March 7, 2027, per FedRAMP Public Notice NTC-0014. **SCIP-139 — PCI DSS 6.3.3 gap assessment corrected to be severity-aware:** * The 6.3.3 compliance-gap assessment previously reported a Gap on any confirmed open CVE regardless of severity, overstating non-compliance against a standard that does not require it. Gap now triggers only on critical severity or a CISA Known Exploited Vulnerability of any severity; other confirmed open vulnerabilities report as Needs Review rather than a compliance gap. * Version-unconfirmed matches no longer produce a Gap on their own — they report as Needs Review (unconfirmed version matches), so a finding SCIP cannot confirm applies to the deployed version is not presented to an assessor as a failure. **SCIP-143 through SCIP-149 — PCI DSS v4.0.1 control-mapping accuracy:** * 12.3.3 and 12.3.4 corrected. Both shipped rows previously described variants of 12.3.4's subject, leaving 12.3.3's real requirement (cryptographic cipher suites and protocols reviewed at least every 12 months) unrepresented while a result was still reported against its identifier. The technology-review check is now correctly identified as 12.3.4, and 12.3.3 is present and honestly marked not assessed rather than reported against the wrong control. * 10.2.1 corrected to 10.2.1.1 to match the content actually assessed (individual user access to cardholder data) rather than the broader parent requirement. * 11.3.2 now discloses that Approved Scanning Vendor status is not verified by the check, so a Pass cannot be read as confirmation that an ASV performed the scan. * 6.4.1 now discloses that its manual-review path was effectively sunset on March 31, 2025 and that an automated solution is required per 6.4.2. * 10.7.1 now discloses that the requirement applies to service providers only, with 10.7.2/10.7.3 identified as the equivalents for all other entities. * Requirement-family titles corrected to the official PCI DSS v4.0.1 wording for Requirement 6 ("Develop and Maintain Secure Systems and Software") and Requirement 12 ("Support Information Security with Organizational Policies and Programs"). * Upgrade path: environments that ran an earlier build carry a stale compliance-status record for the previously mismapped 12.3.3 identifier. A scheduled cleanup removes exactly that one record on upgrade, then no-ops indefinitely. No customer action is required and nothing else in the collection is touched. **SCIP-140 — PCI DSS version labeling:** * Compliance framework labeling updated from "PCI DSS 4.0" to "PCI DSS 4.0.1" across all customer-facing and compliance-evidence surfaces, matching the current published standard. Internal framework identifiers are unchanged, so existing saved searches, lookups, and exports continue to work without modification. **SCIP-138 and SCIP-142 — bundled documentation:** * README detection-rule counts corrected to match the shipped rule set (10 AI/agentic threat detection rules, 9 MITRE ATLAS-mapped, in the summary; 66 rules, 57 ATLAS-mapped, in the detail section). * Stated minimum supported platform raised to Splunk Enterprise 9.4+ and Splunk Cloud. Splunk 9.2 and 9.3 have reached end of life; no functional change for environments already on a supported release. No licensing or crypto surface was modified. bin/scip\_license\_core.py and bin/scip\_ed25519\_verify.py are byte-identical to baseline.

Release Notes:
# Adjutant AI (formerly AI Workbench) — Release notes What's new, improved, and fixed in each release, in plain language. This is the **customer-facing** summary used for the Splunkbase release-notes section; the full technical changelog lives in the project's detailed release notes. **Last updated:** 2026-08-07 > **About version numbers.** Releases once numbered 0.10–0.13 were renumbered to > 1.0–1.3 to reflect production maturity — no behaviour changed. The current release is > **2.2.2** — a maintenance release on top of **2.2.1**, itself a maintenance release on > **2.2.0**'s **Explain a SPL search**, and **2.1.0**'s **Fraud capability** and the **2.0 line** (the deterministic **ITSI Root > Cause Analysis** engine, **resource-consumption monitoring**, and **2.0.7**'s durable memory, > Scheduled Ask and governed integrations), which in turn built on > **1.8.5** (the **CIM Coverage Audit**), **1.8.4** (async playbook execution over MCP > plus the **Outcome Ledger** executive/audit dashboard), **1.8.3** > (a security‑hardening release: OWASP + dependency + anti‑ransomware audit), **1.8.2** (Splunk > Edge Processor data‑quality awareness and keyless Azure OpenAI authentication), **1.8.1** > (support‑diagnosis fixes) and **1.8.0** (agent telemetry & OCSF export, content packs, > all‑tiers data‑quality checks, Splunk 10.x readiness, Dashboard Studio version‑awareness). The > **1.7.0** ServiceNow integration and the **1.5.0 "Data Foundation & MCP OAuth"** themes are > included below. --- ## 2.2.2 "Finish the dashboard" A maintenance release about one thing: runs that did all the work and then ended with nothing on the glass. Every item came from watching real dashboard builds on a live estate, and in each case the assistant's own safety check was the reason the dashboard never appeared. The check was right about the problem and wrong about what to do next — it refused, gave instructions, and the instructions either could not be carried out or cost more of the run's budget than was left. ### Fixed - **Dashboards that were refused are now repaired instead.** When two panels ran the same underlying search, the assistant used to stop and describe a three-step manual fix. The fix is mechanical, so the builder now performs it: it creates the shared search once, points both panels at it, and keeps the fields those panels need. Your dashboards get the efficient shape without the run being interrupted, and the same search no longer runs twice. - **Panels that came back empty next to a search that clearly had data.** When a shared search was widened more than once to serve different panels, each widening discarded the previous one. On one nine-panel dashboard five panels showed "No results found" while the search behind them returned the right events. The widenings now combine. - **A check that asked for the impossible.** A panel that calculates its own value — a formatted date, a derived score — was refused for not finding that value in the shared search, where it cannot exist, because the panel computes it afterwards. Values a panel makes for itself are no longer demanded of the search. The related guidance was also wrong in a way that mattered: panels sharing a search are siblings, not a sequence, so a value one panel calculates is invisible to the others and has to be calculated where all of them can see it. - **A failed publish threw away the work it told you to fix.** The message on a validation failure said the dashboard was still open for editing and warned against starting over. It had in fact been discarded, so the repair failed and the assistant rebuilt every panel from scratch — which on one run quietly changed a correct detection into a different one. The dashboard now genuinely stays open when publishing fails. - **One special character could cost an entire dashboard.** A "≥" written as `≥` in a panel's explanatory text made the whole dashboard invalid, discarding a run of around forty steps that had already produced four working searches. Special characters in text are now handled safely no matter which one is used. - **An empty shared-search reference was treated as a real one**, producing a confusing refusal at publish time that asked for a search with a blank name. ### Improved - **Detections are now held to what you asked for.** New guidance covers the ways a detection can look perfect and point at the wrong event — quietly matching a wider set of events than you described, being loosened until it finally returns a row, discarding the field that distinguishes one event type from another, or dropping the amounts and account numbers an analyst needs before the result reaches the table. A rule that renders beautifully and flags the wrong event is worse than one that returns nothing, because nothing looks broken and nobody checks. The assistant now reads its own result back against the raw events before handing it to you. - **"No results" is no longer accepted as proof a detection works.** For a rule whose job is to match something, an empty result proves only that the syntax is valid — "this does not happen in your data" and "this rule cannot detect it" look identical. The assistant now establishes which of the two it is found before telling you, and runs over a period that actually covers the evidence it has already located. - **Sequence detections ("A, then B, then C") are built correctly.** A common shortcut for expressing order silently sorts alphabetically instead of by time, which can make a rule return nothing on a textbook-perfect match. Ordering is now derived from timestamps. ### Changed - **"Create / Update user template" are now "Create / Update user playbook"**, matching the Playbooks tab they belong to. Existing private playbooks you authored are unaffected; the old entries are retired so you are not offered both. --- ## 2.2.1 "Proven" A maintenance release, and every item in it came from running 2.2.0 against a real estate rather than from reading the code. One new capability came along with the fixes. ### Fraud rings your risk threshold cannot see (Enterprise, fraud-analytics) Risk-based alerting adds up one entity's score across many events. A fraud ring is the opposite shape: many entities sharing one thing. Because those are different questions, no amount of threshold tuning finds a ring. Seventeen mule accounts each earning fifteen points against a threshold of forty are seventeen well-behaved customers, since the risk was split seventeen ways and no single account ever crossed. Lower the threshold and you get seventeen false positives, not one ring. This release adds the query that asks the other question: group by the shared attribute instead of by the account. Nothing new has to be collected, because fraud risk rules have always recorded the linking attribute alongside the score. It simply was never read back this way. It is rarity-weighted, which matters more than it sounds. Ask only "what is shared" and the answer is always the corporate proxy that everybody sits behind. Shared attributes are ranked the same way the Fraud Ring Mapper ranks them, so a shared password hash and a shared IP are never treated as equal evidence, and values that are simply infrastructure are shown separately rather than quietly removed — a short list should not be mistaken for a clean estate. It is also honest about one thing it cannot know. It counts accounts that some rule already scored, which is not the same as how many accounts exist that share the value. So it hands you the search that settles it against your real data, and until you run that, it labels its own confidence as provisional instead of guessing. If you cannot name a starting account, the Fraud Ring Mapper will now find candidates for you before it starts walking. ### Fixed - **Money laundering was graded ready on two weeks of data.** Structuring is a run of individually unremarkable deposits and layering is a graph, so neither is visible in a short window however complete the feed is. Our own use case catalogue has always said to grade retention as well as fields; the grader printed that note and never acted on it. History is now graded, and a use case whose data does not go back far enough is capped at partial with the shortfall named. It is worth separating from other gaps, because it is the one you close with a retention policy rather than an onboarding project. On our demo estate this moved money laundering from ready to partial. - **Every ServiceNow tool call failed** with an internal error reference and no explanation. A tenant lookup returned a dictionary and the calling code expected a pair. - **The fraud readiness dashboard.** Four defects, found by running it rather than reading it. The readiness lookup was private to our own app, so when a dashboard was generated into a customer app the summary panel could not resolve it and rendered empty — which reads as "nothing has been graded" rather than "you cannot see it from here". The audit's own verdicts were being re-graded on the way to the screen, so nine computed verdicts became eight different ones. The coverage audit could not reach the dashboard builder at all, so nothing enforced that a panel must return data before it goes on the glass, and an empty panel on a fraud dashboard is read as "nothing wrong". And no fraud dashboard mentioned data quality: no ingestion check, no TrackMe, no Cribl or Edge Processor. A readiness grade computed over a feed that is arriving late or half delivered is a confident answer about the wrong data, and it fails towards "you are ready". That panel is now mandatory and appears even when everything is clean, because "we checked and it is healthy" is a finding. - **Asking for a readiness audit in plain English now reaches the readiness audit.** The question our own demo guide tells people to ask did not route to the playbook it names. - **Fraud verdict columns are coloured.** Ready, partial and blocked — and the feed inventory's present and absent — were missing from the status colour map, so those columns could only be coloured by hand and often were not. - **A dashboard opened from a finished session sat on "Loading..."** until you refreshed the tab. The new tab was sharing a browser process with a page that was still busy, so it never got a chance to start. - **The dashboard builder could refuse a fix it gave no way to make.** A publish refusal asked for a base search to be amended, and nothing could amend one, so the assistant looped between rebuilding and hand-editing. There is now a tool for it. - **The write-confirmation prompt asked about writes that could not succeed.** You were approving changes that validation then refused anyway. Validation now runs first, so the prompt only appears for writes that can actually happen. - **Token and cost accounting missed cached tokens.** With prompt caching the provider reports only the uncached part of the input, so an agentic run showed a few thousand tokens next to a cost that looked impossible. Cached tokens are now recorded, priced and shown. This affected what we reported, never what you were charged. - **Test Connection for Azure could only ever time out on a broken network.** Its own retries outlasted the window Splunk Web allows, so you got a bare 504 instead of the staged diagnostic. It now finishes inside the window and tells you which stage failed. ### Improved - **History groups by conversation.** A playbook run and its follow-up replies were listed as separate entries. They are now one entry with the turns nested inside and a combined cost. - **Large tool results no longer inflate every later call.** A stateless chat API re-sends the whole conversation on each tool round-trip, so one oversized result was paid for repeatedly. Results are now bounded before they enter the conversation. --- ## 2.2.0 "Explain" ### Explain a SPL search — free on every tier Point it at a search and get back an explanation you keep. Paste the SPL, name a saved search, or give it a dashboard and let it explain every panel. You get a private dashboard and a private saved search holding the same search fully commented, using native SPL comments so the commented copy is still a real, runnable search rather than a printout. This is on **every tier, including the free one**. Reading somebody else's search is the first thing a new Splunk user needs and the last thing they should have to pay for. **It explains what the search does here, not what the commands mean in general.** Your macros are expanded to their real definitions. `tag=web` is resolved to the eventtypes it actually selects on your system. Lookups are shown with their real columns. Command behaviour comes from your own installation's grammar, so an app-contributed command is described correctly. **And it runs the thing.** The pipeline is split at up to four points and each piece is executed over your sample window, so the walkthrough says "the base search returns 4,812 events with 14 extracted fields; after `stats count by host, status` that becomes 37 rows with 3 fields" using your real names and numbers. A field the SPL references that never appears in the results is flagged — the most common silent SPL bug, and one no text-only explainer can see. A search that returns nothing is bracketed to the stage where it broke. Nothing it could not verify is presented as if it were. Verified and unverified statements are never mixed together quietly. ### "Explain this" is usually "why did this stop working" Those two questions arrive in the same sentence, and reading SPL cannot tell them apart: a search whose data stopped arriving looks exactly like a search that was always wrong. So every run takes a feed verdict for the indexes involved, whether or not the search looked healthy. A source that stopped reporting half its hosts, or is arriving four hours late, still returns rows and still looks right — that is precisely when a check is worth having. When something does look off it goes further: ingestion parsing errors, Cribl Stream and Edge Processor if they front your indexers, and the CIM layer, where a perfectly written search returns nothing because acceleration has not backfilled or the index is not in the data model's allowlist. All of that is available on every tier. The per-field CIM audit still needs Professional, and when it is not available the dashboard says so in place, naming what that audit would have told you. ### Fixed - **CIM Coverage Audit acceleration check.** Since 1.8.5 it reported "not visible to the data model" for every source on every estate, because of how it referenced the sourcetype field in `tstats`. It now reports the real counts. If you have run a CIM audit before and were told acceleration could not see your data, run it again. - **Generated dashboards.** Splunk rejects malformed markup with the single unhelpful phrase "Invalid XML."; the app now says what is actually wrong and repairs the common cases itself. Panels bound to a shared base search are checked for the field-pruning trap that makes a panel render empty, or show a wrong number, while the same search works fine when opened in Search. --- ## 2.1.0 "Fraud" Splunk's own App for Fraud Analytics reaches end of life on 1 May 2027, and it is not alone: the App for Anomaly Detection retired in 2025, standalone UBA ends in January 2027, and the App for Behavioral Profiling froze at Splunk 9.4. Four packaged analytics apps retiring on one path, and their customers have no answer today. This release is that answer. - **Find out what your data can actually support, in about a minute.** The Fraud Data Coverage Audit reads your real events and tells you which fraud use cases you can run today, which are partial and why, and which are blocked with the feed that is missing named. It works out which of your sources is which by looking at what they CONTAIN, not what they are called, because real sourcetypes never match the documentation. Today this answer takes a workshop and three weeks of a consultant. - **The check nobody else makes.** It measures whether your entity keys actually survive from one feed to the next. Ring detection is the payoff use case and it is the one most often declared ready on the strength of the fields being present, then failing because an account or device cannot be followed across the boundary. It also tells you when a feed carries every field perfectly but only knows about a fraction of your customers, which is a different problem with a different fix. - **Count actors, not accounts.** One person can open many accounts using the fact that Gmail ignores dots, and to your signup system they look like many different people. Adjutant knows to collapse those, and knows NOT to do it for other providers, where merging two customers would invent a fraud ring that does not exist. When it links entities it always shows you how rare the shared attribute is, because a shared IP address means nothing behind a mobile network and a great deal on a home line. - **Scoring that fits where you already are.** If you run Enterprise Security, everything goes into your existing risk framework and nothing parallel is built. If you do not, it uses the same field names anyway, so the day you buy ES you change a destination rather than rewrite your detections. - **Behavioural profiling that outlives the app it replaces.** Describe the behaviour in a sentence and get a working indicator, anomaly rule and ranked entity list. It compares an entity against its own history, or against its peer group, which the retiring app could not do. It also watches for a feed dying behind a profile: when that happens the scores simply fade, and fading looks exactly like everyone behaving better. - **Nothing here needs those retiring apps.** Every playbook, tool and piece of knowledge works on a plain Splunk estate. What we took from the retiring apps is their METHOD, not a dependency on them: the risk-contribution model, the behavioural profiling pattern, the entity pivots and the fraud use case catalogue are all reimplemented here and improved. If you do still run either app, importers can lift what you built into the native form, but that is a convenience rather than the point. - **The fraud patterns it now knows.** Signup fraud (many accounts sharing an email, IP, phone, password or bank account), account takeover (brute force against credential stuffing, one address against many accounts, impossible travel, and the profile-change-then-money-movement chain), money laundering (funds converging then dispersing, amounts kept just under a reporting threshold, sanctioned-country exposure), and two narrow verticals in unemployment-insurance claims and controlled-substance diversion. All of it reworded into our own framing, with nothing copied from Splunk's documentation. - **Eight playbooks**, including triage for both public sector claims and financial fraud. Both start by checking the data is actually flowing before offering any verdict, because a quiet fraud queue is either good news or a dead feed, and you should know which. Fraud features need Splunk Enterprise and the fraud licence feature. Where either is missing they stay visible and explain what is needed rather than disappearing. The demonstration dataset has no licence requirement at all, so a trial environment always works. One thing said plainly: Adjutant AI is not a fraud detection engine and does not try to be. It will not decline a card payment in a hundred milliseconds; that is what the dedicated engines are for. It is the layer above them that finds what they miss across channels, connects the entities they cannot, and turns three weeks of investigation into an afternoon with a trail you can hand to an auditor. ## 2.0.7 "Memory, Scheduled Ask & Integrations" Adjutant AI gains a durable memory, a scheduled/unattended surface, and a governed data-integration subsystem — so it stops re-asking, can run on a clock, and can sync a system of record into Splunk under a contract two humans have reviewed. - **Memory — it stops re-asking.** A small, durable, per-tenant memory: **learned facts** (the index a report uses, what "the Cribl search" means for a team) captured the moment they're learned, and **integration watermarks**. Two new Knowledge tabs — **Learned Knowledge** (a confirm queue; promote a fact to the whole Org) and **Integration State** (force a watermark to replay or skip). Unattended runs use **confirmed facts only**; a captured-but-unconfirmed fact can't silently steer a run that writes to a target. Backed up per Org with the daily KV Store backup; a content-pack upload never overwrites it. - **"Templates" are now "Playbooks."** A presentation rename that finishes an inconsistency the engine already had (the alert action was always "Run Investigation Playbook"). No data migration. Explicit **run-mode tags** (`triggered` / `scheduled` / `integration`) replace the old bare `playbook` tag. - **Scheduled Ask.** A new admin tab to run a Playbook on a cron schedule — a **Scheduled Job** (run and deliver a result; Professional+) or a **Scheduled Integration** (read a source, write a target, keep watermarks; `ai-integration` feature). Each is a private, service-account-owned saved search that just *triggers* a governed, single-flighted, bounded run — no per-member scheduler racing over shared state (the DB-Connect-on-search-head-cluster lesson applied). - **Governed integrations.** A **mapping spec** is the contract: a versioned, declarative, lint-checked `source → transforms → destination` record the runner executes deterministically — the model never transforms rows. Author it in the new **Mappings** tab (a visual three-pane pipeline editor with a live sample rail, or JSON), promote it **4-eyes**, and **earn** unattended clearance after a verified run. Schema **drift** is detected deterministically, diagnosed by the assistant, and decided by a human — never a silent rewrite. Records land via **`splunk_writer`** (KV Store / CSV / HEC / spool, per-record routing, a fail-closed destination allowlist from the contract). Two ServiceNow example mappings and a standard mapping-driven integration Playbook ship to clone and parameterize. See `docs/ADJUTANT_MEMORY_AND_SCHEDULED_ASK.md` for the operator guide. ## 2.0.6 "ITSI RCA — Industrialise" The Root Cause Analysis engine reaches its industrialise milestone, and the smaller items deferred from earlier trains are completed. All analysis-only and off by default. - **Recovery verification** — after RCA names a cause, re-check whether the service actually recovered (which corroborates the cause) or is still degraded / newly regressed elsewhere. - **Calibrated confidence** — where enough analyst feedback exists, the engine shows a genuinely calibrated likelihood for a candidate instead of a raw internal score; until then it keeps the existing strength wording (never a made-up number). - **Draft, recommend-only remediations** — RCA can produce reviewable draft fixes routed by cause (restore the feed on the culprit host, fix onboarding/timestamp config, restart a stalled input, correct the monitoring, look upstream, add a KPI). Always a suggestion — never executed. - **Data-driven playbook** — the RCA phase sequence is now a validated, dependency-checked contract rather than a hardcoded list (same order, now extensible). - **Sharper feed diagnosis** — names which forwarder/HEC/pipeline host is the culprit, and adds dedicated Cribl and Edge Processor pipeline-health checks. - **Better lineage & safety** — resolves raw host/IP to canonical ITSI entities via declared aliases; follows saved-search/eventtype references inside subsearches; and hardens the unattended template so it can only follow the unattended procedure. --- ## 2.0.5 "Resource-consumption monitoring" A clear, per-tenant answer to *"how much does Adjutant AI cost to run?"* - **New "Resource Consumption" dashboard** shows the CPU, memory, threads and Splunk search-slots Adjutant AI uses — broken down **by Org and by Org/Business-Unit** and by workload (interactive Ask, unattended RCA, unattended runs, and — soon — scheduled Asks). - **Real per-run measurements.** Unattended work runs in its own process, so the app now records actual CPU-seconds, peak memory and thread counts for each RCA cycle and each automation run, tagged with the Org/BU it ran for. The numbers are content-free (counters only) and always on. - **Honest by design.** Interactive Ask runs inside Splunk's shared handler, where memory can't be pinned to one tenant — so for Ask the dashboard reports search CPU/slots (from Splunk's own audit log, mapped to Org/BU) and token/cost usage, and says so plainly, instead of inventing a figure. Additive and safe; no change to how analyses behave. --- ## 2.0.4 "ITSI RCA — discovery & external fold-in" The ITSI Root Cause Analysis engine completes its discovery train: - **Latent-dependency discovery** surfaces a likely service dependency that isn't declared in your ITSI topology but shows up in the data (shared inputs/entities, at-the-same-moment degradation) — proposed as a ready-to-review suggestion, never created automatically. - **External-AI fold-in** can consult an external AI provider's read of the incident and weigh it in as corroborating evidence — it can strengthen or temper a finding, but never overrides the engine's own deterministic verdict. Analysis-only and off by default. --- ## 2.0.3 "ITSI RCA — data-supply legs" The ITSI Root Cause Analysis engine learns to read a KPI's **data supply chain as distinct legs**: - It classifies where a KPI's data actually comes from — a DB Connect input, a universal forwarder, HEC, an Edge Processor / Cribl pipeline, syslog, or a scripted input — and shows which leg carries the most data ("the largest bar"). - When a feed problem occurs, it can point at the **specific leg** that failed (for example "the DB Connect leg stalled") instead of just flagging the whole index. - Behaviour-drift baselines can now be **seasonal** (same time last week) as well as the 7-days-prior default, so normal weekly patterns aren't mistaken for problems. Analysis-only; changes nothing about how the engine behaves until you opt in. --- ## 2.0.2 "ITSI RCA — KPI Behaviour Analysis" The ITSI Root Cause Analysis engine learns to read **how your KPIs are behaving**, not just whether they are red: - **Every KPI, including healthy ones, is profiled for behaviour drift** — a meaningful shift in a KPI's value that its own red/green threshold may miss (for example, response time slowly creeping up after debug logging was accidentally left on). - **Entity-level behaviour** pinpoints *which* entities are driving a service's degradation, not just that the service is unhealthy. - **Suggested-KPI recommendations**: where the analysis finds a blind spot the current KPIs don't measure, it proposes a monitoring improvement — always a suggestion, never a root-cause claim. All of this is analysis-only and off by default; it changes nothing about how the engine behaves until you opt in. --- ## 2.0.1 "Unattended engine hardening" The unattended investigation engine (the part of Adjutant AI that can investigate an alert with no human watching) is designed to hand the alert back to Splunk immediately and do the work in the background. That is what keeps your alerts fast — but it also means nobody is watching if a background run misbehaves. This release makes sure a misbehaving run always stops, and that you can see it when one does. The engine still ships **switched off**. If you have never enabled it, nothing changes for you. **Fixed** - **A run that keeps failing now gives up instead of restarting forever.** If a background run died, it was put back in the queue and started again — without counting how many times it had already failed. A run that failed every time (a bad playbook, a bug) could restart indefinitely and keep occupying a worker. Runs are now retried a set number of times and then parked as "given up", where they stop consuming anything and wait for a person. - **The per-run time limit now actually applies.** The "maximum time for one run" setting was shown in the configuration, charted on the dashboard and alerted on — but nothing enforced it. Runs now stop when they reach it. - **A stuck run is stopped, not just forgotten.** Previously the engine handed the work to a new run but left the stuck one alive, so two runs could work on the same alert and both spend money. The stuck one is now stopped first. - **Long, healthy runs are no longer interrupted.** A slow-but-fine run could be mistaken for a dead one and restarted underneath itself. Runs now report that they are alive continuously rather than only between steps. **New** - **Limits that protect Splunk itself.** A background run now caps its own memory, CPU and priority, so a runaway run degrades into one failed investigation instead of putting the Splunk platform under pressure. Sensible defaults are set for you; all are adjustable, and each can be switched off. - **You can now see stuck and given-up runs.** A run only reports on itself when it finishes, so runs that got stuck were invisible on every dashboard. The *Pipeline Knobs* dashboard has a new run-health section (stuck runs, given-up runs, runs being retried, and what each worker is doing), and two new optional alerts — **Runner stuck** and **Runs dead-lettered** — tell you without anyone having to look. Both are off by default. **Changed** - The retry setting is now called **`runner_max_attempts`** (it covers every kind of failure, not only runaway runs). The unused `retain_completed_hours` setting has been removed — run history retention is controlled by `queue_retention`. If you set either in a local override, update it. --- ## 1.8.5 "CIM Coverage Audit" When a data source is onboarded but a correlation search in Enterprise Security still comes back empty, or an ITSI KPI never fills, the cause is almost always that the source is not properly mapped to the CIM data model the search depends on. Finding out why is normally a slow, manual walk through the layers. The CIM Coverage Audit does it for you, from your real events and your real search head configuration. **New** - **Audit a sourcetype against a CIM dataset.** Ask, for example, audit cisco:asa against the Network Traffic All_Traffic dataset. You get back how much of the dataset the source covers, and if it does not, which layer is broken: the source is not tagged so the model cannot see it, its index is not on the model's allowlist, a field is missing or under the wrong name, a value needs normalizing, or the accelerated summaries the correlation searches read have not caught up. That last one is the confusing case where CIM works when you test it by hand but your correlation searches fire nothing, and the audit calls it out plainly. - **A fix you can read and deploy.** For each gap the audit produces the exact configuration, checked for validity, shown as your current stanza next to the proposed one, with a note on where it belongs. It never deploys anything itself. You review and apply it, which is what lets you run this where an automatic write to production would never pass change control. - **Honest about what a search head can see.** Adjutant AI runs on the search head, so it reads your search time configuration and the real events, and it is upfront that it cannot read the index time configuration on your indexers. It runs its searches as you, so it can never read data from an index you could not otherwise search. - Three read only helpers to read a sourcetype's search head props and transforms and check where a sourcetype has data. The diagnosis is available on Professional so any platform team can see which layer is broken. Generating the validated fix is an Enterprise feature. It grades against the CIM add on actually installed on your search head. Restart Splunk after upgrading. **Fixed** - **The app opens on the Ask tab again.** If your LLM runs entirely on the search head, with the key held server side (the Splunk proxy mode, an Azure managed identity, or a Bedrock role), the browser never receives an API key. The app used to read that as nothing being configured and jumped to the Settings tab on every launch. It now opens on Ask as intended, and only sends you to Settings when a key really is needed and missing. - **Clearer license status.** When a license is installed but the app cannot confirm it is active on this environment, it now tells you that directly instead of quietly dropping to the free Personal tier. Admins get a pointer to the License page to re-activate. --- ## 1.8.4 "Async playbooks over MCP" Run Adjutant AI playbooks from an AI agent over the Model Context Protocol with a reliable **start → poll → fetch** pattern. A playbook can take several minutes, but AI tool calls are subject to short timeouts you don't control (the MCP server, the client, proxies), so trying to wait for the answer in one call is fragile. Now every call returns in seconds. **New / Improved** - **Start returns immediately.** `adjutantai_start_playbook` (the old `adjutantai_run_playbook` name is removed) hands back a run id at once with a hint on how to poll. - **Check progress** with `adjutantai_get_playbook_status` — queued, running, completed, or failed (a run that hit a recoverable error and is auto‑retrying is reported as still running, not failed), with guidance to stop polling after ~15 minutes. - **Fetch the verdict** with `adjutantai_get_playbook_results` once completed — condensed by default, or the full result on request; a partial result is clearly labelled. - **Tenant‑safe.** One team can't read another team's run; unknown or expired run ids simply return "not found." Run records are kept for 7 days by default. - **Try it out of the box:** start `MCP Example: Read-only Health Check` under Org/BU `DFLT/DFLT` (the read‑only reference playbook shipped on every install), then poll and fetch. Requires the inbound MCP server and the Backend Ask Service to be enabled. No configuration changes. Restart Splunk after upgrading. ### Also in 1.8.4 — the Outcome Ledger (Enterprise) A single screen that answers what a CEO, CISO or auditor actually asks: *what did agentic AI do for us this period, was it any good, what did it save, what did it cost — and can I see the evidence for one run?* It assembles data the app already records (unattended‑run history, analyst agreement, run telemetry, LLM spend) into one executive/audit view. It adds **no new data collection and sends nothing to any external service.** **New** - **The dashboard** (`Adjutant AI ▸ Outcome Ledger`): headline tiles (investigations run without a human, how often analysts agreed with the AI — with the sample size and coverage shown, benign/false‑positive runs auto‑closed, analyst hours saved, LLM spend, typical time to a verdict), the mix of AI conclusions over time, agreement by case type, a weekly ledger, and an **evidence** table you can click through to the full detail of any single run. A footer spells out every assumption so a number is never quoted out of context. - **Safe to hand to an auditor.** What each viewer may see is decided on the server from their own identity — never from the page — and fails closed. In this release the dashboard is for Splunk administrators; scoped, delegated auditor access is the next step. - **Is the AI real, or just performing?** An Efficacy Trend panel puts run volume against how often analysts agreed, over time. If the agent runs more while analysts increasingly override it, the panel says so ("scaling faster than trust") instead of hiding it behind a healthy‑looking headline — and on too little feedback it honestly says the sample is too thin to judge. - **Honest numbers.** Effort saved is shown as time (with the per‑case assumption stated), spend is the real logged cost, and the per‑investigation efficiency signal is token usage — never an invented cost estimate. Enterprise feature. No effect on any existing behaviour. Restart Splunk after upgrading. --- ## 1.8.3 "Security hardening" A security‑focused release. Adjutant AI was put through an independent OWASP Top 10 (web **and** LLM), dependency‑vulnerability, and "AI‑driven ransomware" review. The headline: **no critical issues, no default passwords or keys, no vulnerable components that ship to you, and the assistant cannot be turned into an attack tool.** Confirmed issues are fixed; a plain‑language, reviewer‑ready write‑up ships in the app as `SECURITY_AUDIT.md`. **Improved / Fixed** - **Credentials stay server‑side.** Provider API keys and keyless Azure sign‑in secrets are never sent to the browser or to other users in your tenant. (The free‑tier browser API‑key path is unchanged.) - **Prompts stay in your audit index**, not Splunk's internal logs. - **Stronger multi‑tenant isolation** for investigation results and knowledge sources. - **You confirm every change.** Closing a notable, setting a disposition, an ITSI/TrackMe/ServiceNow write, or overwriting a saved dashboard now asks for explicit confirmation first. Read‑only questions and new private dashboards are unaffected. - **General hardening:** cleaner errors, tighter sign‑in redirects, safer content‑pack imports, email TLS verification on by default. No new features or config changes. Restart Splunk after upgrading. --- ## 1.8.2 "Edge Processor data-quality + keyless Azure OpenAI auth" **Keyless Azure OpenAI (Microsoft Entra ID / managed identity).** Connect Azure OpenAI **without a static API key** — using a Microsoft Entra ID service principal or a managed identity, governed by your Entra tenant. Runs entirely server-side (no token reaches the browser), supports Public and US Gov clouds, and adds a one-click **Test connection** that names exactly what to fix if something is off. Connecting Azure with a plain **API key** still works on every tier; the keyless Entra path is an **Enterprise** capability. --- ### Edge Processor data-quality If your data passes through **Splunk Edge Processor** before it reaches Splunk, some parsing, timestamping, dropping and routing happens *upstream* — where Splunk's own internal logs and feed-health tools can't see it. This release teaches the assistant to look at that hop. - **New "Edge Processor → Splunk data-quality check".** Ask the assistant to check an Edge Processor feed and it reads Edge Processor's own operational metrics (throughput, dropped events, failed destination sends, and queue backpressure) and tells you, in plain language, whether data is being silently lost or delayed before it lands — with a proof dashboard. - **Honest by design.** If Edge Processor telemetry isn't reaching your Splunk yet, the assistant says so and gives you the exact setup steps (on-premises vs Splunk Cloud) instead of inventing a clean bill of health. It reports at the pipeline level and is clear that per-event checks need a small addition to your Edge Processor pipeline. - **Folds into the readiness verdict.** Edge Processor joins Splunk parsing, feed-health, and Cribl as another "is this data actually good?" signal, and can cap the Data Quality Score when it finds upstream loss. - Read-only and available on every tier, exactly like the existing Cribl check. --- ## 1.8.1 "Cleaner support diagnosis" A small maintenance update over 1.8.0 (front-end only). - **More accurate "Report an issue" diagnosis.** The automated issue classifier no longer mislabels a session that finished normally — one that completed and produced its dashboard — as having "run out of tool steps." The suspected-issue summary in your support bundle is now cleaner for healthy, tool-heavy sessions. --- ## 1.8.0 "Agent telemetry & OCSF export, content packs & all-tiers data quality" **New — your SOC can watch the agent (OCSF telemetry).** - **Adjutant AI emits its own activity as OCSF.** Every LLM call, tool / MCP / ServiceNow call, configuration change, unattended run verdict, and **policy refusal** (the proof the controls actually fire) can be written as open-standard **OCSF** events to a Splunk index your Enterprise Security / SOC already watches — mapped to CIM via the community **OCSF-CIM Add-On**. Your SOC monitors our agent the same way it monitors everything else: on-prem, with no cloud egress. - **You stay in control.** It is **off by default** and Enterprise-gated. **You provision and name the index** (the app ships no `indexes.conf`). Routing and content are resolved **per Organisation / Business Unit**; content export is denied by default and never exceeds your audit (DPIA) ceiling, with a server-side redaction check before anything is written. - **See it immediately.** A shipped admin dashboard — *Adjutant AI — Behaviour (OCSF)* — shows the token trend, model mix, tool/MCP egress with identity, the refusal and finding feeds, and a per-run drilldown, all on raw OCSF (no CIM Add-On required). **New — update Adjutant's content without waiting for a whole new app release.** - **Content packs.** Almost everything Adjutant does well lives in its **content** — the skills, knowledge, and playbooks. A **content pack** is a single, versioned file that lets us ship a corrected or improved content set straight to your install, and lets your admin apply it safely — no Splunkbase re-vetting cycle for a content fix. - **Your changes are protected.** Applying a pack **upgrades only the items you haven't changed**. Anything your team has customised is left exactly as-is and clearly listed, never silently overwritten — and your Org/BU scoping is always preserved. After an import you get a per-item report, and the list of items that need manual reconciliation is downloadable as a CSV. - **Safe by design.** Every pack carries an integrity check, so a tampered or truncated file is refused. Imports live on the **Backups** page, which also shows which content version you're currently on — run a backup first and you can roll back in one click. - **Retire without deleting.** A pack can mark an item **retired** — it stays installed but is hidden and switched off everywhere (it can't be picked, run, or used by the assistant). An admin can re-enable it at any time by removing the tag. **Improved — data-quality checks for everyone, and Splunk 10.x readiness.** - **Data-quality ingestion checks are now available on every edition, including the free tier.** Checking whether a feed is actually landing and parsing correctly — on `index=_internal`, through **TrackMe**, and through **Cribl Stream** — is a baseline capability now, not a Professional add-on. - **Ready for Splunk Enterprise 10.2 and 10.4.** The app declares Python 3.9 **and** 3.13 compatibility and has been audited against the 10.x platform changes (dashboards, the web framework, KV Store). Your admin still completes the standard KV Store engine migration as part of any 10.x upgrade. - **Smarter Dashboard Studio building.** The assistant now works from a single, version-aware map of what Dashboard Studio supports on **your** Splunk version — it won't reach for a chart type your version can't render, and when your Splunk is newer than what we've documented it builds conservatively and verifies the result. **Fixed.** - **Fewer false "the dashboard is blank" errors.** A heavy Dashboard Studio dashboard that renders fine but slowly is no longer wrongly reported as blank — the assistant confirms the panels actually returned data before deciding, so it stops wasting a retry on a dashboard that was already correct. A genuinely blank dashboard is still caught. - **TrackMe panels only when they belong.** Fixed a rule that pushed a TrackMe feed-health panel onto every generated dashboard (and used a lookup that fails outside the TrackMe app). The assistant now adds a feed-health panel only when it's actually relevant, using a method that works in your app. --- ## 1.7.0 "ServiceNow integration" (included in the 1.8.0 release) > **Renamed to Adjutant AI.** The app is now **Adjutant AI** (formerly "AI Workbench"). > This is a **display-name change only** — the in-app title (the easter egg now lives on > the dot of the "i" in **Adjutant Ai**), the app label, the documentation, and the > assistant's own self-description all say **Adjutant AI**. Nothing functional changed: > the Splunk app id, your saved searches/dashboards/models, KVStore data, and generated > artifact names are unchanged, so the upgrade is seamless. **New — run playbooks automatically, and from other Splunk apps.** - **On a schedule or on an event.** A playbook can run **unattended** on a schedule (a "morning health check") or in response to a Splunk event — an alert, an ES correlation search, or an ITSI episode. When an event triggers it, the affected thing (the host, user, or entity in the alert) is handed to the playbook automatically, so it investigates exactly what fired. Two ready-made (disabled) examples are included to copy. - **Adjutant AI as a building block for other apps.** Other Splunk AI agents can now ask Adjutant AI to **list** and **run** your playbooks through a small, safe interface (an MCP server). Only playbooks you mark **MCPready** are exposed, every call must name the Org/BU it is for (which must be a business unit you have set up) as a safeguard, and runs go through the same governed, bounded service — never an open door. This interface is **off by default** — turn it on with one setting. When on, the tools can also appear inside **Splunk's own MCP Server**, reachable on the normal Splunk web address (no special port needed); you authenticate with a standard Splunk token. A ready-made, read-only **example playbook** ships enabled so there is always something to see the moment you switch the interface on. **New — "Report an issue" support packaging (all editions).** - One click on any conversation (per-turn 🐞, the Ask panel, or the new **Help tab**) packages exactly what happened — versions, the resolved prompt, the tools and model used, the generated dashboards/searches, and every error and warning — into a single file. - **Safe by construction:** secrets are stripped before anything leaves the browser, and the file is **encrypted** to the support key, so it's safe to send over any channel. - It even **tells you what kind of problem it looks like** and matches known issues, so simple cases are solved without a back-and-forth. - **Send it your way:** download it and attach it to your own ticket, use the built-in support form, or email it. The **Help tab** (Report + Documentation + About) is always reachable — even if the app is locked by licensing. **New — ServiceNow, done properly** (Professional + the `servicenow` feature). Read incidents, changes, problems and the **CMDB/CSDM** in plain English — with bounded blast-radius / dependency traversals ("what's the blast radius if this CI fails?"). Turn a Splunk alert, ITSI episode or ES notable into a rich, deterministically rendered ServiceNow incident and **write the number back** to the originating object (a re-fire updates, never duplicates; the closed-incident policy is configurable). **Security incidents (SIR)** with MITRE ATT&CK, off until an admin enables them. Two transports (REST **or** a ServiceNow MCP server), plus TISC threat-intel enrichment — all server-side and allowlisted, so ServiceNow can never block the assistant. *(Verified against the documented APIs and unit-tested; final certification is on a live ServiceNow.)* **New — run playbooks automatically, and from other apps.** Playbooks can run **unattended** on a schedule, or from a Splunk alert / ES correlation search / ITSI episode (the triggering entity is handed to the run). Adjutant AI can also expose **list / run** over an inbound **MCP server** (off by default, MCPready-only, Org/BU-scoped) — reachable inside Splunk's own MCP Server on the normal web address, with a standard Splunk token. **New — "Report an issue" support packaging (all editions).** One click packages a failing conversation — secret-stripped and **encrypted client-side** — with an automatic problem classification, plus an always-reachable **Help tab** even when the app is licence-locked. **New — Cribl Stream data-quality awareness** (Professional+). Reads Cribl's own forwarded logs and metrics to surface the timestamp / parse / dropped-event problems that happen *inside Cribl, before Splunk can see them* — the "green in Splunk but timestamped wrong" blind spot — folded into one readiness verdict. No Cribl Lake or Search required. **New — LLM reliability: retry, fallback & circuit breaker** (Enterprise). A brief provider hiccup (503 / 529 / rate-limit) auto-retries within a time budget; a per-config **circuit breaker** stops hammering a provider that's down, then probes for recovery; and an ordered **fallback** transparently switches to your next provider (and tells you which it used). Two new admin dashboards — **LLM Health** and **AI Activity** — plus per-user / BU / org concurrency caps, all conservative and off the critical path. **New — live model & cost catalogue (all editions).** Models and prices come from a runtime catalogue that updates without an app rebuild; **automatic model discovery** (Professional+) keeps it current without ever logging your keys; an Enterprise admin screen adds price overrides and manual model registration for private gateways. **Fixed.** Generated Simple XML dashboards now share a single base search across panels (faster) and get a top data-ingestion health panel; corrected a 3× Opus price over-charge (now server-side authoritative, with Opus 4.8 and Fable 5 included). --- ## 1.5.0 "Data Foundation & MCP OAuth" **New:** connect to **OAuth 2.1‑protected MCP servers** (authorization‑code + PKCE for interactive, client‑credentials for unattended; tokens held server‑side, never in the browser — see [MCP_OAUTH.md](MCP_OAUTH.md)); **onboard new data sources** — describe a source or attach a sample file and get a deployment‑ready add‑on package; a **"is my data parsed correctly?"** ingestion/timestamp check that reads Splunk's own internal logs; generated config **validated against your instance** and given a **0–100 Data Quality Score** (A–F); and attach a local sample file in Ask (only the file name is audited, never contents). **Improved:** works with the newest OpenAI "reasoning" models incl. Azure GPT‑5.4 / GPT‑5.4‑mini (auto‑detects the request format); more reliable generated dashboards; generated objects use the **`aiworkbench`** name tag; and Audit‑tab improvements (Business Unit column/filter, local‑timezone timestamps, reliable token/outcome capture). --- ## Earlier releases (1.0.0 – 1.4.3) - **1.4.3** — Clearer guidance and plain-language fixes when a free-tier LLM key hits its provider limits (e.g. Groq token-per-minute caps, Gemini zero-quota keys); the LLM config screen flags these up front. - **1.4.1** — Per-feature capability licensing with edition badges (Professional / Enterprise / MSP); gated features show a padlock, and nothing you created is ever deleted when a tier changes. Turn-level audit logging made reliable; more robust dashboard generation. - **1.4.0** — The assistant reads your own Splunk **live** (real search commands + installed visualizations) instead of guessing; Splunk Security Essentials detection content integrated. - **1.3.3** — TrackMe integration end-to-end (feed-health awareness + actions) with richer built-in platform knowledge. - **1.3.2** — First Splunkbase 1.x release: packaging and permissions hardening. - **1.3.1** — Fixed Org/BU edits dropping fields; safeguard to keep bundled playbooks correct after upgrades. - **1.3.0** — Real, per-Organisation audit logging of every AI interaction (Professional+). - **1.2.0** — Splunk Security Essentials content tools for playbooks. - **1.1.1** — Cisco Deep Time Series Model (CDTSM) playbooks: pre-trained anomaly detection and forecasting via the AI Toolkit, each with a proof dashboard. - **1.1.0** — Multi-tenancy and the Organisation / Business-Unit editor overhauled for clearer, safer tenant scoping. - **1.0.0** — The knowledge layer: ground answers in your organisation's own conventions. *(Releases before 1.0 are early pre-release history and are omitted here.)* --- ## Known issues - **Open the assistant from inside another app.** Adjutant AI is a "host shell": reach it from a navigation-menu entry inside Search, Enterprise Security, ITSI, or your own apps — not by clicking the app tile directly. Everything it creates lands in the namespace of the app you opened it from. - **Some Data Foundation features need self-hosted Splunk.** The configuration-reference grounding and config-package generation (1.5.0) read files on the Splunk server, so they are unavailable on Splunk Cloud; the assistant says so and continues with what it can. --- *When a published fix resolves a tracked GitHub issue, it is summarised here with its issue number — for example: "Fixed: a dashboard panel could display raw HTML markup as text instead of formatting it (#123)."*


Short Description:
A workbench for Splunk, not just a chatbot. Analyse, correlate and build across SPL, dashboards, alerts, AI Toolkit / MLTK, ES, ITSI and TrackMe through tools that understand each one — plus any MCP server you add. Pick your LLM: Anthropic, OpenAI, Azure, Groq, Gemini, Bedrock, Ollama, OpenRouter. Multi-tenant, multi-tier (Free, Pro, Enterprise, MSP).


Description:
Adjutant AI (formerly AI Workbench) is a generative workspace for Splunk — not a chatbot bolted onto search, but a real workbench where you investigate, analyse and build with tools that understand Splunk. It is a host shell: it has no use-cases of its own, deriving everything from the Splunk app a user opens it from and their roles. Install once on the Search Head, then embed it in the apps your users already live in — Search, ITSI, Enterprise Security, your SOC and MSP customer apps. Users never leave the app they came from, and artefacts land in that app's namespace. Ask in plain English. Get back validated SPL, Simple XML and Dashboard Studio dashboards, alerts, lookups, reports and Splunk AI Toolkit (MLTK) machine-learning pipelines — grounded in your running Splunk (your knowledge objects, live command syntax, CIM models), run for real before they are saved, owned by the calling user. The depth is the difference. Where a generic MCP-only assistant talks to Splunk through one broad door, Adjutant AI ships fine-grained, Splunk-aware tools across Core, Enterprise Security, ITSI, TrackMe, ServiceNow and the AI Toolkit, each scoped to one job and run under your existing Splunk ACLs. Extend it with HTTP tools or any MCP server. New in 2.1 — a fraud capability that starts by telling you what you cannot yet detect. The Fraud Data Coverage Audit grades your estate against nine use cases (including AML) and returns ready, partial or blocked with the specific blocker, identifying event families by what events contain rather than by sourcetype name. Entity resolution runs before scoring, because risk accumulates per entity. Generated rules are weighted contributions with readable reasons, emitted into Enterprise Security's risk framework where it exists and into RBA's own field vocabulary where it does not. Nothing generated is ever enabled or scheduled. New in 2.0 — ITSI Root Cause Analysis with no LLM in the answer. It walks your real dependency graph, verifies the data behind every KPI, scores the evidence transparently, then lets an LLM narrate. The same evidence always gives the same answer. A red KPI on a dead feed is a data problem, and it names the forwarder, HEC, DB Connect, Cribl or Edge Processor leg at fault. Plus durable memory, scheduled playbooks, governed integrations, and per-tenant resource-consumption reporting. Your SOC can watch the agent: LLM calls, tool and ServiceNow calls, config changes, unattended verdicts and policy refusals emitted as OCSF events to an index Enterprise Security already watches. On-prem, no cloud egress, off by default. Bring your own LLM: Anthropic, OpenAI, Azure OpenAI, Groq, Gemini, Bedrock, Ollama (fully offline) or OpenRouter — server-side, so keys never leave the search head. Multi-tenant by design. Free, Professional, Enterprise and MSP tiers, self-serve and air-gap-friendly.

* Adds | honeylabssearch, a generating command that queries the honeypot dataset directly. * Nine modes: raw sensor events with every recorded field, literal substring search over captured request payloads, CVE exploitation, ASN profiles, attacker rankings, attack volume over time, and TLS, JA4, JA4H and SSH fingerprint searches. * Adds a second dashboard, Explorer, covering the dataset on its own terms.


Short Description:
Threat intelligence from live honeypot sensors, in SPL. Enrich any IP field with a verdict, ASN, ports and first and last seen, or query the dataset directly: raw probes, request payloads, CVE exploitation, JA4 fingerprints, top attackers. Plus two hourly threat feeds. Free API key gives 500 lookups a day; no key gives 10.


Description:
HoneyLabs runs open-source honeypot sensors on the public internet. Nothing reaches them by accident, so every connection they record is a scan, a probe, a brute-force attempt or an exploit. There are no false positives to filter out, because there is no legitimate traffic to confuse them with. This app puts that dataset inside Splunk. Two search commands. The first enriches addresses you already have. Point it at any field holding a public IPv4 address and it annotates every event: index=firewall | honeylabs field=src_ip | where honeylabs_events > 0 It writes back verdict, verdict_key, network_type, events, first_seen, last_seen, country, asn, asn_org, rdns, top_port, ports, exploit_hits and reference, each prefixed honeylabs_ so nothing collides with your own fields. Addresses are de-duplicated per search, so an index carrying the same scanner across ten thousand events costs one lookup. The second queries the honeypot dataset directly, with no local data required. Nine modes cover raw events, captured request payloads, top attackers, timelines, ASN profiles, TLS and HTTP fingerprints, IOC and CIDR lookups, CVE exploitation, and fingerprint population counts. Use it to answer questions your own logs cannot: who else is exercising this CVE, what payload is being sent, which other sources share this JA4 fingerprint. Two modular inputs, shipped disabled, index active exploiter addresses and captured malware staging URLs on an hourly schedule. Neither needs credentials. Two dashboards ship with the app: an overview of what the feeds currently carry, and an explorer for querying the dataset without writing SPL by hand. About the API key. The app installs and runs with no account and no setup, but anonymous use is capped at 10 lookups a day, which is enough to try the commands and not enough to work with. A free key raises that to 500 a day and takes about a minute to create at https://honeylabs.net/dashboard. Paste it into the app's setup page; it is stored through Splunk's storage/passwords, encrypted at rest, and never written to a .conf file. Paid plans go to 50,000 a day. On privacy: a lookup sends only the public IP addresses in your search. Not your index, host, source or sourcetype names, not your Splunk version, not the search string. Private, loopback, link-local, multicast and reserved addresses are filtered out locally before the request is built. The feed inputs are ordinary HTTPS downloads of a public file and disclose nothing at all. Running Enterprise Security? Load the indicator feeds through its own threat intelligence framework so they reach correlation searches and risk scoring rather than only being searchable, and keep these commands for on-demand investigation. Walkthrough: https://honeylabs.net/integrations/splunk-es

item.description:

Release Notes:
**### Version 2.1.4** \* **\*\*Fix: KV Store outage log clarity.\*\*** When Splunk KV Store is unavailable, checkpoint read/write now logs a clear warning instead of the misleading \`HTTPError\`/\`int\` TypeError from Splunk's helper. Collection continues using the configured start\_datetime window; restore KV Store for incremental checkpointing. **### Version 2.1.3** \* **\*\*Fix: Proxy lookup crash on Splunk 9 / Python 3.7.\*\*** \`get\_proxy()\` used \`rest.simpleRequest(..., raiseAllErrors\=True)\` without a top-level handler. When Splunk's REST layer failed, it could raise \`TypeError: '>\=' not supported between instances of 'HTTPError' and 'int'\`, aborting alert collection before any JupiterOne API call. Proxy lookup now uses \`raiseAllErrors\=False\`, validates status codes explicitly, and falls back to direct (no-proxy) requests. **### Version 2.1.2** \* **\*\*Fix: Deferred host resolution.\*\*** Host lookup no longer runs during input initialization (which triggered a GraphQL call before collection and could crash the entire run). Host is resolved at collection time from checkpoint, alert webLink, or base URL fallback. \* **\*\*Fix: Host fallback from GraphQL base URL.\*\*** When no checkpoint or sample alert exists, derive \`apps.\*\` host from the configured \`graphql.\*\` base URL so collection can proceed on fresh inputs. \* **\*\*Fix: Safer traceback formatting.\*\*** Guard against malformed tracebacks that caused \`TypeError: '>\=' not supported between instances of 'HTTPError' and 'int'\`. \* **\*\*Ops: Version marker in logs.\*\*** Each input run logs \`(TA version 2.1.2)\` so deployed builds are easy to verify. **### Version 2.1.1** \* **\*\*Fix: Alert collection HTTP error handling.\*\*** Replaced Splunk \`send\_http\_request\` (which raised \`HTTPError\` before status codes could be handled, and could mask the real error with a secondary \`TypeError\` during traceback formatting) with direct \`requests\` calls using the same proxy pattern as the JupiterOne search custom command. \* **\*\*Fix: Safe error trace logging.\*\*** Added defensive traceback formatting so HTTP and connection failures log the actual status code and response body instead of failing with \`'>\=' not supported between instances of 'HTTPError' and 'int'\`.


Description:
The JupiterOne Add-on imports and enriches JupiterOne Alerts, allowing you to access this data in Splunk. It collects alert data directly from JupiterOne, parses the data and extracts valuable data so that you can trigger your own notable alerts in your Splunk account. It also provides workflow actions that allow you to link back to entities in JupiterOne or search your JupiterOne account for any field value in Splunk, regardless of entitytype and now supports a Custom Command so that you can execute a J1QL query directly from Splunk and display the response from JupiterOne in your Splunk account.
